Issue 014, phase 4: `scripts/issues/014-integrate-menu-tui-into-scripts.md`.

**Before:** `backup-conversations` was command-line only. To back up a project you had to know its path, and transcripts always went to the project's own folder (or its fixed archive).

**After:** `backup-conversations -I [project]` opens a menu:
- **Do:** Back up every conversation, or Back up the newest conversation.
- **Project:** every project Claude has conversations on record for, most recently active first, with how many each has (`/path/to/proj (12)`). A folder you name that has none is shown as `(none on record)`.
- **Transcripts go to:** the project's own folder, or "Another folder..." to type a path. A typed folder is offered again next time.
- **Go:** runs the choice.

The panel below the items shows the last four lines of the last run and the newest transcript of the project under the cursor (the issue's "sample transcript"). Each run is shown as it goes. The menu then reopens with a one-line note, such as `Backed up proj-one: Exported 2 log(s), 0 failure(s).` or `Failed: Claude has no session folder for ...`. `q` leaves.

There are new command-line options too: `--newest [project]`, and `-o/--output <folder>`, which works with any mode.

## How

- `interactive_mode` rebuilds the menu each time round. Go runs `bash <this script> --all|--newest <project> [-o folder]` and keeps a copy of the output for the panel.
- `known_projects` and `project_of_session_folder` build the project list.
- `newest_main_log` is shared by `--newest` and the project list.
- `newest_transcript_in` picks the preview.
- `transcript_dir_for` is now the one place that decides the output folder (`-o`, then the special-folder table, then `<project>/llm-transcripts`).
- `main` takes `-o/--output` out of the arguments before reading the mode, so it may stand anywhere.
- `-I` is handled before `main`, in the run-when-executed block.
- The README documents `-I`, `--newest`, `-o` and the new environment seams. Issue 014 gets a What Happened entry for phase 4.

## Decisions

- **One Go button and a "Do" list, as in #211 and #213.** `menu_run` only reports that an action was pressed, so `menu.lua` stays untouched.
- **Every menu choice is also a command-line option, and Go runs the script itself.** A menu run is therefore logged and checked exactly like a hand-run one, with stop-on-error, the lock and the log's `tee`, and it has no separate code path to drift. This is the same principle as #213's `--day`/`--at`.
- **The project list comes from the `cwd` recorded in the session logs, not from the session folders' names.** A folder name can't be turned back into a path, because every character that isn't a letter or digit became a dash. A folder is listed only when its name is the one Claude Code would give that `cwd`, and that folder still exists. Session folders whose project is gone are left out.
- **The project you name keeps the spelling you gave it,** links included (`realpath -s`), because Claude Code files sessions under the spelling a session started in. With no project named, the current folder is chosen if Claude has conversations for it, else the most recently active project.
- **"Newest" means the main log written to last.** It's read from file times, not from the times inside the log.
- **The output folder is typed at a prompt after the menu closes.** The menu has no text field, and its flag items take numbers only. An empty answer does nothing and says so.
- **The menu runs outside `main`'s `tee` to the log,** because it needs the terminal. It turns off `set -euo pipefail`, which the menu library isn't written for. Each backup it starts still runs with stop-on-error.
- **The scratch tiers' roots can be overridden** (`EXEC_TIER_ROOT`, `ARTIFACT_TIER_ROOT`, the same names as `libs/ensure-ram-tiers`). The test then writes nothing to the real `/tmp/ai-stuff-scripts` or `/dev/shm/ai-stuff-scripts`. With neither set, nothing changes.
- **The subtitle note is cut to the terminal's width,** as in #213. Each script has its own copy of that helper; moving it into `lua-menu.sh` would touch the library that #179 is changing.
- **The "Last run" panel shows four lines,** because the menu gives every panel but the last at most four.

## Merge notes

- **Conflict with #211 and #213.** Like them, this PR appends a `## What Happened` section to issue 014, so every one merged after the first will conflict at the end of that file. Resolve it by keeping each entry under one heading and trimming each closing "still to do" line to what is still open.
- **#174** also edits `backup-conversations`, in other lines. A test merge of the two branches has no conflicts.
- This PR doesn't touch `validate-issues` or `delta-version/`.

## Tested

`bash scripts/tests/test-backup-conversations-interactive.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: 22 passed, 0 failed (about a minute). It uses a scratch session store with two projects and one whose folder is gone, a scratch toolchain folder, and scratch tier roots.

**Command line:**
- `--newest` exports only the newest conversation.
- `-o` sends a sweep to the named folder and not to the project's own.
- The tiers and the log are made under the given roots.

**The menu, driven in a pretend terminal and checked on the replayed screen:**
- Go backs up every conversation, and the note reads `Exported 2 log(s), 0 failure(s).`
- Both projects are listed with their counts, and the gone one isn't.
- The panel shows the project's newest transcript.
- "Newest" exports one conversation, the right one.
- Choosing the other project backs up that project only.
- A typed folder gets the transcripts and is offered next time.
- A named folder with no conversations is shown, Go says why nothing was done, and nothing is created in it.

The real scratch log is not written to, and `/tmp` is clean afterwards.

**Existing tests, run with a scratch `SCRIPTS_DIR` and scratch tier roots:**
- `test-transcript-export-guards.sh`: 14 passed, 0 failed.
- `test-backup-conversations-sessions.sh`: 31 passed, 2 failed. The two failures are "unreadable log", and they fail the same way on main. The test makes a log unreadable with file permissions, which root (this container) can still read. They are not caused by this PR.

Hero-less-moba issue 505, spawning onto a wave. **Stacked on #201**: the base is `claude/hlm-commander-tests`, so the diff shows only this change.

**Before:** A hero bought onto a wave appeared at the wave's anchor, which is its front. That is the first place the enemy's line touches, and it made this the best destination in every case, not just the aggressive one.

**After:** The hero lands one body's width behind the wave's **rearmost living member**, down the middle of the road. This is what the issue intends: the hero arrives behind its escort and walks up into the fight.

## How

- `place_hero` in `src/054-commanders.lua` finds the wave's living member furthest back along the lane. "Back" is measured against the direction the team walks, so it is mirrored for team 2.
- The hero is placed `radius(rearmost) + radius(hero)` behind that member, with across = 0. It borrows the member's path index as the lookup hint.
- If a wave has living members but none in its lane, that is an error. It cannot happen in practice, because buying onto an empty wave is refused before this point.
- Docs updated: issue 505 (current behaviour), `docs/012-hero-units.md`, `src/054-commanders.info.md`, and `tests/075-the-commanders.info.md`.

## Decisions

- **Follow 505's intent: land behind the rearmost living member. Chosen by Claude, open for Ritz.** Recorded the same way in issue 505.
- **The gap is the two bodies' radii, down the centre of the road.** That is the walk's own spacing between bodies; I added no new tunable number. Chosen by Claude, open for Ritz.

## Tested

- **This replaces the #201 check** "and arrives in that wave's lane, at the wave's front", which pinned the old behaviour. It is now two checks:
  - "and arrives in that wave's lane, just behind its rearmost living member";
  - "and the far team's hero lands behind its own wave, from the other end".
  - Both require the hero to be behind every living member, and less than 20 units behind.
- With the old placement restored, both new checks fail: the hero lands about 91 units in front.
- `tests/075`: 42 of 42 on the pinned seed and on seeds 1–3.
- `./run-tests . code` with `HLM_SEED=20260826`: invariants 84 passed, 6 failed (the same 6 as main); sandbox 17 of 17.
- `./run-tests . docs`: 0 problems.
- **No match changes.** Bots buy only at the library or a tower, and no scenario buys onto a wave. Not seen on screen.

body:
## Before

No map ran on the 60 Hz frame that the input model needs. The engine already had periodic timers (206) and argument doors (309), but nothing put the two together. The phase 5 progress file listed all of 501–508 as open, with no note of what each one waits on.

## After

- **`src/maps/input-poll.map`**: an engine timer writes a tick into the map's argument door every frame. A `frame_next` station turns each tick into the next frame number, carried round a loop like `counting.map`'s count. Each frame fans out to `read_buttons`, `read_sticks` and `read_touch` stubs, which answer an empty state stamped with the frame. After them come `button_events`, `stick_events` and `touch_events` stubs that tally the frame.
- **`src/boxes/095-input.c`**: those boxes, plus the value types every surface will use (`struct button_snapshot`, `stick_snapshot`, `touch_snapshot`).
- **`program_argument_every`** (068): an engine timer aimed at a program's argument door.
- **`src/system/096-input.c`**: `input_poll_start` loads the map, brings it up and arms the timer one frame from now. `input_poll_stop` disarms it.
- **Issue 501** moved to completed, with answers and what happened.
- **`issues/phase-5-progress.md`** now holds the **scoping note**. Phase 5 sorts into three groups:
  - **Twin now:** the event logic of 502–504, then 505.
  - **Blocked on unmerged stacks:** 506 and 507 (406 is #35, 408 is #48).
  - **Device:** 508, plus the device halves: the boot call, the GPIO/ADC/I2C reads and calibration.

## How

The frame number cannot live in a box, because boxes keep no state. So it rides a wire that points back to its own station. Only one frame number is ever on that wire, which means frames are made one at a time and in order. The timer is the engine's own periodic timer: each deadline is the one before plus a period, and when every core is idle the device sleeps until that deadline.

## Decisions (each one Ritz can overturn)

1. **A `.map` file, not JSON.** Step 1 says JSON, but phase 3 settled on `.map` files compiled into the image.
2. **The frame number is a loop.** A `constant` puts 0 on the loop once, and the timer's tick value (`1`) carries no meaning.
3. **The period is 16 666 667 ns**, so the frame runs 20 ns per second slow (1.7 ms per day). Making it exact would have meant changing the engine's timer. Deadlines are still measured from the previous deadline, not from when the work finished.
4. **Frame numbers count deliveries, not periods.** `engine_timer_missed` counts the skipped periods, and those get no frame number. On an idle device nothing is skipped.
5. **`kernel_main` does not call `input_poll_start` yet.** The device's cores do not run the engine until 202. The function is linked into the kernel image and ready.
6. **One box file for every input surface (095).** The value types are declared once there. 502–504 add to the same file rather than redeclaring the types.
7. **`input_poll_stop` only disarms the timer.** The program stays placed, with the next frame waiting on its loop. `program_remove` takes it away.
8. **New file numbers 095–097**, above every number used on any open soren-ds branch (the highest was 094). `.file-index-counter` still says 59, as it did before; I left it alone.

## Tested

- **Twin debug and fast:** all 10 test programs pass, including the new **097** (33 checks).
- **097 under load:** passes 4 of 4 runs with eight busy loops competing for the four CPUs.
- **ASan** (with #36's fix applied locally): 097 passes. 054 aborts, as documented. **075's spread check failed once and passed on rerun.** That is the flake #205 fixes; it is on main and is not touched here.
- **Kernel cross-build** (aarch64, ld.lld): links, with `096-input.c` and the new boxes in the image.

Issue 014, phase 1: `scripts/issues/014-integrate-menu-tui-into-scripts.md`.

**Before:** `filesystem_scanner.sh` was command-line only. To change the cron day or time, you had to edit variables at the top of the script.

**After:** `filesystem_scanner.sh -I [folder]` opens a menu with these sections:
- **Do**: Scan now, Install cron job, Remove cron job, Preview schedule.
- **Folder**: the folder you named, the folders scanned lately, the default folder when none was named, and "Another folder..." to type a path.
- **Cron day**: every day, or one weekday.
- **Cron time**: hour and minute.
- **Go**: does what the Do list says.

A panel below the items shows this script's installed cron line and the last picture of the folder under the cursor. After each step the menu opens again, with a one-line note in the subtitle. `q` leaves.

The command line also gains `--day DAY` (`daily`, `sun`..`sat`, or `0-7`) and `--at H:MM`, for use with `--install-cron` and `--show-cron`.

## How

- `interactive_mode` rebuilds the menu each time round, runs the chosen step, and records a note.
- `prepare_output` is split into two functions: `prepare_tiers` and `output_path_for`.
- `main_execution` calls `remember_folder`, which keeps the last eight folders in `recent-folders.txt` in the RAM tier.
- Every `crontab` call goes through `$CRONTAB`.
- The README documents `-I`, `--day`, `--at`, the recent list and the overrides.
- Issue 014 gets a What Happened entry for phase 1.

## Decisions

- **One Go button and a "Do" list, as in #211.** `menu_run` only reports that an action was pressed, not which one, so `menu.lua` stays untouched.
- **`--day` and `--at` flags.** Every schedule the menu can set can also be set without it, and without editing the script.
- **Recent folders are kept in the RAM tier** (`recent-folders.txt`, last eight, most recent first). Every scan adds to the list, whether or not it ran from the menu. The list starts empty after a reboot, like the pictures beside it.
- **The default folder is offered only when no folder was named.** The tests always name one, so they never touch `/home/ritz`.
- **The cron day is a radio list, not a multistate item.** On main, a multistate item can't be given a list of choices until #179 merges.
- **The time is two number fields, checked before anything runs.** A bad value leaves the crontab alone and says why in the subtitle.
- **The subtitle note is cut to the terminal's width.** A long path would otherwise run over the menu's frame.
- **Each step runs in a subshell.** The old functions call `exit`, so this way a failed step ends that step, not the menu.
- **`SCRIPTS_DIR` and `FILESYSTEM_SCANNER_CRONTAB` can be overridden from the environment.** This lets the test use a scratch RAM tier and a stand-in crontab. Without them, nothing changes.
- **Left as they were:** `install_cronjob`'s `/tmp/temp_crontab_$$` file. The panel only shows when the terminal has rows to spare below the items, which takes about 46 rows.

## Merge notes

- **Conflict with #211.** #211 (014 phase 3) also appends a `## What Happened` section to issue 014, so whichever PR merges second will conflict at the end of that file. Resolve it by keeping both entries under one heading. Each entry's closing line names the phases still to do, so trim that line to phases 4 and 5.
- No other open PR touches `filesystem_scanner.sh`. This PR doesn't touch `validate-issues` or `delta-version/`.

## Tested

`bash scripts/tests/test-filesystem-scanner.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: 27 passed, 0 failed (about two minutes).

**Command line:**
- A scan writes its picture into the RAM tier and nothing into the scanned folder.
- The recent list keeps order and drops repeats.
- `--day wed --at 23:30` installs `30 23 * * 3`, and `--show-cron` reads it out as "Every Wednesday at 11:30 PM".
- Installing again replaces the line.
- A bad day or time exits 1 and leaves the crontab unchanged.
- Uninstall removes the line.

**The menu, driven in a pretend terminal and checked on the replayed screen:**
- Scan the named folder, a remembered folder, or a typed folder.
- Install for Friday at 7 (`0 7 * * 5`), with the note and the panel showing the line.
- An hour of 99 is refused and the crontab is unchanged.
- Remove takes the job out.

No real crontab, RAM tier or `/home/ritz` path is touched, and `/tmp` is clean afterwards. `bash -n` passes.

Builds the first half of hero-less-moba issue 213, "What the lane can afford", as 213a. **This changes what a wave is.** 213b, still to come, will change what upgrades are.

**Before:** Every wave in every lane was the same seven bodies: a captain plus melee and ranged bodies split by the commander's `melee_share`. Bodies carried no equipment, and nothing decided a wave's composition.

**After:** Beside its captain, each wave is drawn from its lane's deck of tickets. There is one deck per lane per team.
- Four kinds are appended to the unit table as rows 19–22: heavy infantry, light infantry, skirmishers and archers. Cavalry is not built, as specified.
- Each body walks out in a kit drawn at birth. The kit's weight is its cost.
- A drawn body discards its cost off the deck. A missing kind's meter walks one out undrawn.
- No wave holds three of a kind.
- The pile shuffle is the one specified: 3, 4, 5, 4, 7.

## How

- **`src/076-the-lane-deck.lua`:**
  - `begin` builds every deck and pile-shuffles it.
  - `draw_wave` meters first, then draws until the purse is spent. It sets aside a third of a kind, or a card for a half the commander has filled, then settles the books: meters, discards under the undrawn tickets, and the purse refilled up to its ceiling.
  - `pile_shuffle` is pure.
- **`src/039-waves.lua`:** `queue_wave` takes its composition from `draw_wave`. Line bodies get the front role and missile bodies the back. Because the deck orders heavy first, heavy lands nearest the centre of its rank and light toward its ends. Skirmishers come before archers, so the archers stand furthest back.
- **`src/032-the-world.lua`:** a `soldier.kit` bit mask. `give_body` folds in the row's `kit.carries` plus the optional pieces in the mask, so `restamp_team` keeps kit through a boon. `wear()` errors on an unknown piece.
- **`assets/025`:** rows 19–22, `M.equipment` and `M.deck`. The dead `melee_count` and `ranged_count` are removed.
- **Elsewhere:** the arena passes kit 0, and `042` hangs `lane_deck` and calls its `begin`.

## Decisions — all chosen by Claude, open for Ritz

Every number lives in `M.deck` or `M.equipment` in `assets/025-unit-table.lua`.

- **The purse is counted in tickets turned.** H12 says cost is "how much of the deck a choice consumes", not a price checked against a balance. So every card off the top costs a point: the one drawn, the ones discarded for it, and any set aside.
  - It is not a separate currency; I judged a second number would be a price by another name.
  - Income is 18 a wave, it saves up to 36, and it starts at 18.
  - The last body may take the purse into debt.
- **Starting tickets:** heavy 2, light 12, skirmishers 8, archers 6. That is about the old two-line-to-one-missile ratio, with heavy rare. With heavy at 4 tickets, heavy came out at about one a wave in my measurement.
- **Max tickets** is twice the start. So the meter's doubling threshold means four waves missing, for every kind alike.
- **A resource point is two units of weight**, rounded up, never less than one. Light infantry in spear and leather costs 1; full heavy kit costs 4.
- **Equipment:** mail, shield, war blade, sword, spear, cap, leather, javelins and bow. Each adds to health, armour, damage, range or speed. Base rows are near-identical ("the differences are equipment rather than statistics").
- **The meter** fills by an entry's tickets each wave the kind is missing and resets when it walks out. A body spawned by the meter is not drawn but still pays its discards.
- **"Never three"** is a cap of two per kind per wave, as the issue's step 7 test asks. The body cap is 8.
- **The commander's `melee_share` is kept** as the maximum share of a wave that may be line, against the body cap. This keeps F40 ("a commander is a mixture and a captain"). Docs 005 and 011 and the commander table now say so.
- **Kit streams are per lane per team but named for the lane only.** Both sides' first waves are therefore identical and an untouched match is still a mirror, while neither team's draws depend on the other's. A stream named per team broke the opening mirror in wave one.
- **Siege-surge streams and arena formations still use melee and ranged.**
- **Purse 18 gives about 4.9 bodies a wave, not 6.** The never-three cap holds the line at four, so a bigger purse buys heavier waves, not larger ones. I erred toward the old strength.

## Tested

- `./run-tests . docs`: problems 0. The census is 60 of 80 (+1 for 213).
- New suite `tests/077-the-lane-deck.lua`: 25 of 25. It covers the shuffle passes, the mixture over 300 waves, never-three, the body and commander caps over 1,200 waves, a poorer and lighter wave after heavy, discards going under the undrawn tickets, the meter, cost following weight, the mirror, exact kit stats, and kit surviving a restamp. Passes on 25 seeds.
- `./run-tests . code` with `HLM_SEED=20260826`:
  - Invariants: 85 passed, 5 failed, against main's 84 passed, 6 failed. Two of main's failures now pass (the bend and the boon).
  - One new failure: "the keyframes hold it near the match that was played", 106.2 against 101.8. That check is seed-sensitive on main too: main fails it on seed 13, and this branch fails it on 20260826 and 11, out of 11 seeds tried. Replay determinism ("reproduces the match at every keyframe") passes. I did not touch the check.
  - Sandbox: 17 of 17.
- Scenes: the same 2 failing claims as main.
- **Balance note:** on the pinned seed the long scenario ends at tick 15,389 instead of 14,484, and team 1 wins instead of team 2.
- The viewer ran 900 frames under a stubbed LÖVE without error. **Not seen on screen.**
- **Merge note:** `run-tests` gets a suite hunk in the same place as #154 and #201; keep all of them. The census lines conflict with every census-moving PR; the total if all merge is 75 of 80. File numbers 076 and 077 follow #201's 075.

**Stacked on #208** (`claude/state-daemon-dir`, issue 052). The tests need a daemon running in their own folder, and only that fix makes that possible. Merge #208 first; until then this diff also shows #208's commit.

Issue 014 (scripts), phase 3: an interactive mode for `state-daemon.sh`. Issue 014 stays open for phases 1, 4 and 5.

## Before:

`state-daemon.sh` was command-line only. To see what it held you ran `dump`, and changing anything meant typing one command per key. There was no way to watch values change.

## After:

- `state-daemon.sh [DIR] -I` opens a lua-menu screen listing every key as `key = value`; the description line shows the full pair.
- A **Do** list picks what **Go** does:
  - Refresh
  - Set a key: key and value are asked for at a prompt once the menu closes
  - Delete the checked keys: check them with space
  - Clear all keys: asks y/N
  - Watch
  - Stop the daemon
- When the daemon isn't running, the list offers **Start the daemon** instead.
- After each step the menu reopens with fresh values and a one-line note in the subtitle (for example "Set delta" or "Deleted 1 key(s)"). `q` leaves.
- `state-daemon.sh [DIR] watch [secs]` redraws every key every `secs` seconds (default 2) until a key is pressed.

## How

- New functions in `state-daemon.sh`: `daemon_running`, `dump_pairs` (sorted), `watch_mode` and `interactive_mode`.
- Each loop round rebuilds the menu from a fresh `DUMP`, runs it, and acts on the chosen Do item.
- `lua-menu.sh` is sourced only in `-I` mode.

## Decisions

- **One Go button and a Do list, not a button per action.** `menu_run` reports only that an action was pressed, not which one. Telling actions apart would mean changing `menu.lua`, which #93 and #197 are rewriting, so I left it alone.
- **Set uses a plain prompt.** The menu has no free-text field. A key must be one word with no `=`, because the daemon takes the first word of a SET line as the key and `dump` writes `key=value`.
- **Clear asks first; delete acts only on checked keys.**
- **Watch is its own loop.** The menu can't redraw on a timer. Without a terminal on standard input, watch keeps to its interval rather than spinning on end-of-input.

## Tested

- `bash scripts/tests/test-state-daemon-interactive.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: 16/0, about a minute. It drives the real menu in a 30x100 pretend terminal (`script` plus typed keys) against a daemon in a temp folder, then asks the daemon what it holds. It covers:
  - deleting a checked key, and the keys listed with their values;
  - setting a typed key and value, and the note on the reopened menu;
  - refusing a key that contains a space;
  - clear answered n, then y;
  - stop from the menu, then start offered and working, with state kept;
  - watch from the menu, left with a key;
  - `watch` on its own without a terminal.
  
  The test stops every daemon it started when it exits.
- `bash scripts/tests/test-state-daemon.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: still 21/0.

No other open PR touches `state-daemon.sh`, its README or issue 014; merges clean with #93 and #197. This branch doesn't edit `validate-issues`.

Housekeeping: scripts issues 10-004 and 10-007 move into `completed/`.

## Before:

Both issue files have said "Completed" since 2025-12-23, and `issues/10-progress.md` lists both as completed. The files still sat in `issues/`, so tools that count `completed/` (the progress dashboard, the validator) counted them as open.

## After:

Both files are in `issues/completed/`, each with a short What Happened saying what was checked.

## How I decided they belong to scripts

Phase 10 is neocities-modernization's numbering, so I checked whether these issues should be moved across instead. They should stay in scripts:

- neocities-modernization's own `completed/10-005-…` says 10-004 was **moved to `scripts/issues/`** on purpose.
- `scripts/issues/10-progress.md` tracks phase 10 here.
- 10-007's fix is in scripts' own library: `parse_flag_value` in `libs/menu.lua`, tested by `libs/test-menu-lib.lua`.
- 10-004's library half (`menu_set_command_config` in `libs/lua-menu.sh`, the preview in `libs/menu.lua`) is in scripts. Its `run.sh` half is in neocities-modernization.

So I moved them within scripts and didn't touch neocities-modernization.

body:
Stacked on #141 (`claude/soren-ds-card-faults`): the test pulls the twin's card mid-move, which #141 adds, and the box builds on #117's `append_path`.

## Before
`append-path` (413) can build a file larger than one value, but between appends the file holds only the appends so far. A reader of `/drawings/cat` could see half a saved drawing. docs/011 tells apps to write to a temporary path and rename it over the destination, but no box could rename a file.

## After
- New box **`move_path(from, to)`**. The file at `from` takes the name `to`, replacing any file that had it, and any missing directories on the way are made. It answers 0 or a negative code.
- A program builds a big file under its own name with `append_path`, then moves it over the name readers use. Readers see the old file or the whole new one.
- A link at either end moves, or is replaced, as itself; the name moves, not what it leads to.
- A directory is neither moved nor replaced, and the status says so.
- New issue 414 is filed and closed here. docs/011, the note in 413 and the phase-4 progress file are updated.

## How
`files_move` (078) works in three steps, in an order that is safe to interrupt:
1. It removes the old name.
2. It points the new name at the chain: one block write onto an existing entry, or a new entry.
3. It frees a replaced file's clusters.

If the card is pulled after step 1, the chain belongs to no name and the destination is as it was. The lost space is what `fsck.fat` reports. There is never a moment when two names share one chain.

`fat_dir_remove` now marks the short entry deleted before the long-name pieces. This applies to deletes too. An interrupted removal then leaves orphan pieces, which readers already skip. Before, it could leave the file alive under a short name the card made up.

## Decisions
- **Old name first.** Writing the new name first leaves, if interrupted, two names on one chain. Deleting the temporary file afterwards would then free the destination's bytes. Old-name-first only risks the temporary file.
- **If the new name can't be written for a reason other than the card** (a directory full to FAT's limit), the old name is put back and the status says why.
- **Links are moved, not followed**, as a laptop's `rename` does. Otherwise "replace the link `latest`" couldn't be expressed.
- **Directories are refused.** Moving one means rewriting its `..` entry, and no app needs that yet.
- **It answers 0 or a negative code**, like `write_path` and `append_path`, so all three can feed the same consumer.

## Tested
- New `twin/tests/094-test-move.c`, 27 checks:
  - moves to new names and onto existing files, with the replaced file's clusters given back;
  - links moved as themselves, and a file moved over a link;
  - refusals for directories and the root;
  - the same file spelt two ways, left as it was;
  - every slot of a long name freed when it moves away;
  - the card pulled after each of a replacing move's 21 blocks and each of a long-named, new-directory move's 49. Every time the destination was old or moved, never torn; no two names shared a chain; no file was left under a made-up name;
  - the box: three `append_path` calls build a file under its own name while the reader's name keeps the old one, then `move_path` swaps it in.
- Mutation checks, both caught:
  - adding the new name before removing the old shares a chain;
  - removing the long-name pieces first leaves made-up names.
- Full twin suite in debug and fast: 15 programs pass.
- ASan (gcc, with #36's patch applied locally) is clean on 079, 081, 083 and 092–094.
- The aarch64 kernel builds.
- `fsck.fat` isn't installed here, so its checks were skipped.

Issue 052 (scripts, new): `state-daemon.sh` ignored the folder it was given. I found this while looking at the script for issue 014's interactive mode.

## Before:

`state-daemon.sh DIR start` said "Daemon started", then `state-daemon.sh DIR set a 1` answered `ERR:daemon_not_running`.

The daemon is a new run of the script (`bash "$0" _daemon`), and DIR was not passed on to it. So it used `/tmp/state-daemon`, while the client commands looked in DIR. When that default folder did not exist, `mkfifo` failed and the read loop spun on the missing pipe, writing an error line to `DIR/daemon.log` many times a second. `start` only checked that the process was alive, so it reported success. Running the new test against the old script leaves four such daemons spinning.

## After:

- The daemon runs in the folder it was started for.
- A daemon that cannot make its request pipe logs why and exits.
- `start` reports success only when the request pipe exists and the PID file names the daemon, waiting up to 2 seconds. Otherwise it says "Failed to start daemon (see …/daemon.log)", stops the process and exits 1.

## How

`STATE_DAEMON_DIR="$DIR" nohup bash "$0" _daemon …` in `start_daemon`, a guard around `mkfifo`/`chmod` in `daemon_loop`, and a wait loop in place of the fixed half-second sleep.

## Decisions

- **The folder goes through the environment**, which the daemon already reads, so the `_daemon` command line is unchanged.
- **"Started" means listening, not just alive.** The bug was a live process that could not listen.
- **A failed start stops what it started.**

## Tested

`bash scripts/tests/test-state-daemon.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: 21/0, about 4 seconds. It covers:
- start in a temp folder: the pipe and PID file land there, and ping reaches the daemon;
- set, get, count, list, dump, del (and the non-zero exit for a missing key), status and save;
- stop, then state surviving a restart, then clear;
- a folder where the pipe cannot be made: start reports failure and exits 1, no daemon is left, and the log stops growing and says why.

Against the old script, 18 of the 21 fail. The test stops every daemon it started when it exits, because the old script's daemons cannot be found through their folder.

No open PR touches `state-daemon.sh`. This branch does not edit `validate-issues`.

Issue A01 (scripts), step 8: incremental updates for `git-history.sh`. The issue stays open because one step is left, the per-project `src/cli/` symlink, which needs the owner's projects.

## Before:

Every run rebuilt each `phase-X-commits.md` from scratch. That costs eight git calls per commit. The issue's "Supports incremental updates" box was unticked.

## After:

`git-history.sh -a -u` (or `--update`) reads each phase file before replacing it. A commit whose section is already in the file is copied as it stands; only the missing commits are formatted. The header, the total and the statistics are worked out afresh each time. The result is the same file a full run would write. The report says how many commits were new, e.g. `(5 commits, 1 new)`.

## How

- The commit index now also records each commit's short hash (`SHORT_HASH`). It gets this from the same single `git log` call (`--format=@@%H %h`), so no extra git calls are made.
- `git_history_load_sections` reads the old file's sections below `## Commits`. Each section is keyed by the hash in its `## [<hash>]` heading.
- `git_history_format_markdown` copies a section when it has one, and formats the commit otherwise.
- `generate_phase_history` writes to a file beside the old one and moves it over the old one when done.

## Decisions

- **Sections are matched to commits, not appended after "the last commit seen"** as the issue's sketch suggested. Commits come from every branch (`git log --all`), so a merge can bring older commits into the middle of the list. Matching keeps the order a full run gives.
- **No `.git-history-state` file.** The phase file is the state. A separate record could disagree with a file that was deleted, edited or restored.
- **Old sections are kept as written**, so a hand edit inside one survives `-u`; a plain run still rewrites everything. If a short hash grows longer as the repository grows, it no longer matches, and that commit is simply formatted again.
- **`--update` is opt-in.** A plain run behaves as before.

## Tested

- `bash scripts/tests/test-git-history-update.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: 14/0. It builds a git repository in a temp folder and checks:
  - an update matches a full run after new commits, and again after a merged side branch with `--stats`;
  - a hand edit inside an old section survives `-u` and is gone after a full run;
  - the new-commit counts in the report;
  - `-u` with no file yet behaves as a full run;
  - no temp files are left behind.
- On main the test fails at once, because `-u` is an unknown option there.
- I also ran it on the real `scripts/` history: `-a -s` followed by `-a -s -u` gave the same four phase files as a fresh full run, and the update took 1.5 s against 4.6 s.

Conflicts: #99 also edits A01 (it adds a `Blocks:` line), and the two merge cleanly. No other open PR touches `git-history.sh`. This branch doesn't edit `validate-issues`.

body:
## Before
Tests 049 (task ring) and 075 (kinds, doors, launch) failed whenever the laptop was busy with other work.
- **049** ran for minutes instead of about a second, until the runner's limit killed it.
- **075** read counts short of what was sent ("4670 9130 23501" out of 40000), or saw spread split 1000 / 1000.
- With eight busy loops running alongside, the unchanged 049 and 075 both hit a 100-second timeout every time.

## After
The suite passes with every CPU busy, and every original check still holds; 075 adds two.
- With eight busy loops running, 049 takes about 4 s and 075 under 1 s.
- The whole suite passed three times in a row under that load, in 7 to 15 s.
- On a quiet host, 049 takes what it took before: 0.7–1.2 s, against 0.7–0.9 s for the original.

## How
**The lock (the main cause).** `spin_lock` is a ticket lock, which serves waiters in arrival order.
- On the device that is correct, because nothing takes a core away from running code.
- On the twin, each core is a thread. A busy host sets runnable threads aside for whole time slices.
- When the thread holding the next ticket was set aside, every waiter behind it spun away the CPU that thread needed. The lock moved once per time slice: 049 measured about 130 operations a second.

The fix:
- Two new platform hooks: `platform_spin_wait(word, seen, turns)` for waiters, and `platform_spin_wake(word)`, which the release calls when others are queued.
- **Device:** waits exactly as before (the `yield` hint) and never sleeps.
- **Twin:**
  - A waiter spins while the queue keeps moving.
  - After 1024 turns with no movement, it sleeps in the kernel (futex) on the lock's now-serving word.
  - The release wakes the sleepers. A thread woken from sleep runs promptly, where one merely set aside waits its turn.
- The lock is still a ticket lock, served in order, on both builds.

**075's spread check.** It relied on the feeder outrunning a slow destination. On a busy host the feeder doesn't keep up, every value is handled before the next arrives, and ties split the values evenly.
- Now the slow destination is held: its second input has no source while the values arrive.
- Values arrive in batches of 100, and the program settles after each batch.
- After the last batch, the slow destination gets its input and works through its backlog.

**075's settles.** Every settle that 075 relies on is now checked, with a one-minute limit. A settle returns as soon as the engine is idle, so this costs nothing on a quiet host.

## Decisions
- **Change the twin's way of waiting, not the lock.** Issue 204 chose arrival order on purpose. A twin running a different lock would stop testing the one the device runs.
- **Sleep instead of yield.** Yielding after a short spin still timed out with eight busy loops: the host gives the CPU to whatever is runnable, which is rarely the thread holding the next ticket.
- **Count turns from the queue's last move, and sleep after 1024.**
  - 128 turns, counted from the start of the wait, made 049 ten to twenty times slower on a quiet host.
  - 4096 turns was slower under load and no faster when quiet.
- **Holding the slow destination makes the spread check reliable, but it no longer exercises one part of spread's look:** the count of runs already queued for a destination (issue 308). That part only shows when runs pile up in the ring, which a test can provoke but cannot guarantee.
- **The `freopen` line in 075 carries the same fix as #13,** so the test builds here. The identical change should merge cleanly.
- **I did not regenerate the `.info.md` files for `025-platform.h`, `042-platform-device.c` and `026-platform-twin.c`,** to avoid clashing with #20. Regenerate them after both merge.
- New issue **216** records the measurements.

## Tested
- Full twin suite, debug and fast: passes with the host quiet, and passes three times running with eight busy loops added.
- Mutation check: making spread ignore its look fails the reworked check (1000 / 1000).
- ASan (gcc, with #36's patch applied locally): 049, 051 and 075 are clean.
- The aarch64 kernel builds.
- Under ASan, 054 stops in `port_page_checksum` while parking. That is expected: `twin/Makefile` notes that parking, which works on whole pages, isn't meaningful in the ASan variant, because every block there comes from the host's allocator. It is the same on main and not touched here.

> **Merge #181 first.** This branch is built on `claude/040d-audit`, which is built on #119. Once #181 is merged, set this PR's base back to `main`.

**Why that base:** this needs #181. The rotation records each removal on the audit trail, and `verify` and `diff` must read those rows to tell a pruned backup from a lost one. Both commands come from #181, so this can't go any lower.

## Before
Every `approve` left a backup under `backups/`, and nothing ever removed them. Step 7 of the 040d issue ("rotate old backups, keep last 100") was still open.

## After
`claudemd-revise.lua prune [--keep=N] [--yes]`:
- keeps the newest N backups (default 100), going by the date in each backup's name;
- also keeps, however old, every backup a rollback still needs: the last approval of each proposal that is approved now;
- without `--yes`, only lists what it would remove (`would remove  P002-….md`), with a count of what it keeps;
- with `--yes`, removes those backups and writes a `pruned` row to `audit.tsv` for each one.

`diff` on a pruned backup says "was pruned on DATE, so this change can no longer be shown", where it used to say the backup was missing. `verify` does not count a pruned backup as a problem.

## How
- Only files named the way `approve` names its backups (`ID-DATE-TIME.md`) are considered. Anything else in `backups/` is left alone.
- `verify` now builds a proposal's timeline from status rows only (proposed, approved, rejected, rolled-back). A `pruned` row therefore never counts as a "last action" against its status.

## Decisions
- **Rotation is a command, not something `approve` does by itself,** so nothing is ever deleted unasked. Listing without deleting is the default, and `--yes` deletes.
- **Backups a rollback needs are never pruned,** so rotation can't take away an undo. The ones it removes belong to rolled-back proposals and earlier approvals, and only `diff` uses those.
- **No checkpoints**, as agreed with the coordinator: `audit.tsv` is enough to rebuild every status.
- **Issue files:** only 040d's own file gets a status section. `040-…md`, `PRIORITY.md` and `progress.md` are unchanged, because #181 and its siblings touch those lines.

## Round 8 additions (second commit)
- **`proposals.tsv` is append-only.**
  - Each row is written once, when the proposal is filed. A proposal's status is now its last status row on `audit.tsv`.
  - `approve`, `reject` and `rollback` no longer rewrite the file. The row keeps the status it was filed with.
  - State folders from before, whose file was rewritten in place, still read correctly. `verify` checks that any status they kept agrees with the trail, and that no proposal is filed twice.
  - The broken-state test now edits a filed status to `approved`, not `pending`, because `pending` is what every row is filed with.
- **`conflicts`** is the conflict analysis from step 6 of 040d. It is a report and decides nothing. It lists:
  - approved guidelines in one file that share two or more topic words, where one is a "don't" and the other is not;
  - corrections recorded since an approval that touch two or more of its topic words;
  - approvals rolled back, and guidelines proposed again after.

  Matching is by shared words, so a contradiction in other words can be missed. Deeper detection belongs to 040e.
- The storage stays TSV, not the JSON lines in the issue's sketch. Changing the format would orphan trails already kept.

## Tested
- `test-claudemd-revise.sh --dir …`: **81/81 passed** (57 before, 12 for rotation, 12 for the append-only log and `conflicts`). The new checks cover:
  - nothing to prune under the default;
  - listing only, without `--yes`;
  - keeping a backup for rollback;
  - removing oldest first;
  - leaving files with other names alone;
  - `--keep=0`;
  - the audit rows;
  - `diff` saying a backup was pruned;
  - `verify` passing after a prune;
  - never removing the backup a rollback needs;
  - a bad `--keep` value.
- `validate-issues delta-version`: 93 findings before and after, all pre-existing.

## Waiting until after merges
Left out because #181 and its siblings touch the same lines. To do once #181 and this PR are merged:
- `040-dynamic-claudemd-revision-system.md`: a status note saying 040d is covered (queries, provenance, diff, verify, rotation, append-only proposals, conflicts report). It should also consider moving 040d to `completed/`.
- `PRIORITY.md`: the 040d row.
- `progress.md`: an entry for 040d at the top of the recent list.

Issue 201: a map inside a box. This is stacked on #200 (`claude/ceramic-history`), because it adds a third change to the workshop's history and picks up the next file numbers (017, 018) from the shared counter.

## Before

`inside PATH` on a box only had to point at a directory with an `org.map` (M14). Nothing checked that the inner map had anything to do with the box, and the board stopped at the top level.

## After

- `src/017-inside.lua` checks every box that has an inside, all the way down, by rules N1-N6 (docs/002, "Maps inside boxes"):
  - N1: the inner map is a valid org.
  - N2: a box can't have an in port and an out port with the same name.
  - N3: each in port is an inner outside that something takes in from and nothing sends out to.
  - N4: each out port is an inner outside that something sends out to.
  - N5: **the inner map has no other outside**.
  - N6: no map can be inside itself, and loops are found by real path.
- `./validate-org` runs these checks whenever any box has an inside, and refuses the org if a problem is found.
- `./blocked-board`, under a source that holds a map, prints one line per level: `inside making, first: cutting (ready, reach 1)`.
- The workshop example: `making` now holds `making/` (cutting, then joining). That was added by the proposal `making-shows-its-inside`, applied as change 3, so `./replay-history` still rebuilds the map exactly.
- docs/005: Q6 gains the reasoning for N5, and there is a new Q10 on how state crosses a box's wall. Q10 is now answered, and the answer is filed as issue 204 (see Decisions).

## How

- The inner map's outsides are named after the box's ports, so lining the two up is plain name matching.
- 017 loads the reader and the board as libraries. 007 and 008 load 017 lazily, only when a box has an inside.
- Every module's run-as-program guard now fires only once, using a `CERAMIC_MAIN` global. This touches 007, 008, 010, 012, 013 and 015.
  - Without it, `validate-org` re-ran 007's main inside itself until the stack overflowed: 017 loads 007 while 007 is the program, and the old guard only matched arg[0].

## Decisions

- **Outsides are named after the box's ports, not after the parent's sources.** A team's map then doesn't change when the box is rewired upstairs. It only changes when the box's own ports change.
- **N5: an inner map reaches the world only through its box.** Without it, a team could open its own door to the river, and the parent's door rules (an outside eye and a week) would never see it. That would be the vision's hidden complexity, one level down.
- **N2 refuses a box whose in port and out port share a name.** From inside, the two would be the same outside.
- **The board looks inside sources, not inside blocked boxes.** A source is where the waiting can be undone. Asking which part of a source to unblock first is the useful question. A blocked box's inside only explains a wait that is already explained upstream.
- **Each map keeps its own `org.state`, and in this PR the box's wall does not carry state across.** How it should was first left open as Q10.
  - Q10 has since been answered, and a second, doc-only commit records the answer in docs/005: a fed port is fed at the inner doors that take from it, and a finished inner map makes its box done. Both are derived when the maps are read, never stored twice.
  - A box with a map inside can't be marked done by hand while that inner map is unfinished. That will be a new state rule, S5.
  - The answer is filed as **issue 204** (`issues/204-state-crosses-the-wall.md`), with the roadmap and phase 2's progress updated. It is not built here: the stack waits on merges first.
- The workshop's inside arrived as a proposal, so nesting goes through the same agreed-change path as everything else.

## Tested

- `./run-tests` passes under luajit and lua5.4:
  - map and board: 72;
  - proposals: 60;
  - monorepo and page: 38;
  - history: 18;
  - the inside: 18.
- The new tests cover:
  - one refusal for each of N1 to N5, with N3 and N4 each refused in several ways;
  - N6, both for a map directly inside itself and for a loop through a child;
  - a problem two levels down being found from the top;
  - the board descending two levels;
  - `./validate-org` refusing an org whose inside is bad.
- History test 016 now expects three steps, including in its unnumbered case.
- Every example validates, and the workshop's history explains its map exactly.

> **Merge #126 first.** This branch is built on `claude/053-shared-components`. Once #126 is merged, set this PR's base back to `main`.

**Why that base:** #126 adds `todone.lua`, whose `--json --each` output is this tool's input, and `config/component-synonyms.conf`, which tier 2 reads. Without #126, nothing would produce the input. I didn't use #176 (`libs/component-names.lua`): that would make the stack one PR deeper just to share about 25 lines. Those lines are repeated here instead; see Decisions.

## Before
`todone.lua` (#126) matched component names only by spelling (tier 1) and by the synonym file (tier 2). It ignored typos and near-names like "task executor" and "task queue". It gave no confidence and no statistics.

## After
`scripts/todone-similarity.lua found.json|-` groups todone's component names into clusters, and gives each member a confidence and the tier that joined it:

| Tier | Joins | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | same name ignoring case, spaces, `-`, `_` | 1.0 |
| 2 | one line of `component-synonyms.conf` | 0.95 |
| 3 | likely typo: 1 letter apart (5+ letters) or 2 apart (9+) | 0.8 |
| 4 (`--max-tier=4`) | the local model says **yes** about an uncertain pair | 0.85 |

- The output follows the issue's JSON (`clusters`, `unclustered`, `uncertain`, `analysis_stats` by tier) or a text report.
- Library candidates are clusters planned by at least `--min` projects.
- Nothing is written anywhere.

## How
- **Uncertain pairs** are names that share a word of 4+ letters, where one name sits inside the other, or that are 3 letters apart. These are the only pairs put to the model, at most `--max-asks` (20) per run. The prompt asks for "yes, no or maybe", and the first word of the reply decides.
- **Confidence:** a member's confidence is the weakest link between it and the cluster's first member (the name the most projects plan). A typo of a synonym therefore gets 0.8.
- **Unreachable model:** the remaining pairs are not asked, and tiers 1–3 still stand.

## Decisions
- **A separate script.** It is not built into `todone.lua`, as in the issue's CLI section. That leaves `todone.lua` untouched, so this can't conflict with #176, which edits it. Re-running the clustering also costs no model calls.
- **Only a yes merges.** A maybe (listed at 0.5), an unclear answer or an error is listed under "uncertain" for a person to judge, and is never merged. The spec's own sketch treated a maybe as similar; I didn't, so a weak answer never joins two components. An unclear answer or an error sets exit status 1.
- **Tier 3 thresholds** are tighter than the spec's flat "distance ≤ 2" rule, so short names like gui/tui stay apart.
- **The default is `--max-tier=3`,** so no model is asked unless you request it, as the spec's CLI example has it.
- **`key_of`/`load_synonyms` are repeated** from `todone.lua`. Once #176 is merged, they can switch to `libs/component-names.lua`.
- **Not built:** tier 5 (a large model with code context), `--format=matrix` and `--show-reasoning`.
- **Issue files:** only 053b's file is updated (a status note, plus 7 of 8 criteria ticked). `053-…md`, `PRIORITY.md` and `progress.md` are left alone, because #176 edits the same lines.
- **`brain.lua` is unchanged.** The test runs the stand-in server with a small brain of its own, which gives fixed yes/maybe/no/error answers.

## Tested
- `test-todone-similarity.sh --dir …`: **34/34 passed**. The suite covers:
  - each tier on its own;
  - confidences and tiers;
  - gui/tui staying apart;
  - library candidates and unclustered names;
  - tier 4 yes/maybe;
  - the shared stand-in's unclear answers, which merge nothing and exit 1;
  - an unreachable model;
  - a model error on one pair;
  - `--max-asks`, stdin, shared-only input and usage errors.
- `validate-issues delta-version`: 93 findings before and after, all pre-existing.

## Waiting until after merges
- **Once #176 is merged:** a small follow-up switches `todone-similarity.lua` from its own `key_of`/`load_synonyms` to `libs/component-names.lua`. Not done now.

Covers hero-less-moba issues 501, 504, 505, 506, 507, 509 and 510 (the tests asked for in the round's commander step).

**Before:** No test named any of phase 5's mechanics except the three the invariants already cover (502, 503, 508). The census read 59 of 80. A tower refusal named the tower beside the library whenever any tower between was clear. And every `ability` event read just "ability": the ability's own name was written into `name`, which `raise()` overwrites.

**After:** A new suite, `tests/075-the-commanders.lua`, has 41 checks and runs in the code half of `./run-tests`. Phase 5 is fully named, and the census reads **66 of 80** on this branch. A tower refusal now names the **nearest** clear tower behind. An ability event carries its ability's name in `ability`.

## How

- Every check builds a fresh match with the bots off, then puts bodies exactly where its question needs them. Only the wave check lets the match run, and only until the first waves have walked out.
- **501:** checks that the catalogue is well formed, that seats are dealt the same on both teams, that wallets start empty, that waves rotate through a team's players, and that the bounty ratio is walked exactly.
- **504:** checks that every ability resolves to a condition, an effect and a cooldown. A priest mends once and then waits out its cooldown, a heal stops at full, and an unknown ability is an error that names it.
- **505:** a hero bought onto a living wave lands in that wave's lane at the wave's anchor and stays out of the wave's counters. Enemy and empty waves are refused.
- **506:** a clear tower accepts. A tower with an enemy in its radius refuses, charges nothing and spawns nothing. The refusal names the nearest clear tower behind, or the library when every tower in the lane is under attack. Enemy towers, fallen towers and unknown destinations are refused.
- **507:** a library hero takes the deepest-pushed lane, ties go to the lower lane, and team 2 enters at its own end.
- **509:** each roster has five distinct heroes with no shared ability. Line-killing, stone-killing and mending are all present. No two heroes on a roster have the same bill.
- **510:** two priests with two wounded take one each; with one wounded, both heal it. Claims clear every tick. A druid skips allies already regenerating, and a curse-doctor picks the most-mobbed enemy. A druid behind an unbroken rank of its own cannot cast the moon spike, and can once the rank is gone.
- **The two fixes:** `tower_behind` in `src/054-commanders.lua` now keeps the largest milestone below the refused one. The `ability` event in `src/055-abilities.lua` now uses an `ability` field. Both checks fail on `origin/main` and pass here.
- **Docs:** the run-tests code half, the info file, a "Tested" note in each issue's current behaviour, 510's stale "claim rule not built" line, phase-5 progress, and the 111a and phase-1 census lines.

## Decisions

- **The tests pin what each issue's "Current behavior" says is built, not the "Intended" text where the two differ.**

  - 506: the purchase is refused, not pushed back with a distinct reason code. Recorded in 506.
  - I did not change either behaviour in a test PR.
- **509, the bill check:** I first wrote "no roster is all one price". That contradicts the unit table, which says heroes cost about the same total and differ in the bill's shape. Every hero costs 5 in total. So the check asks that no two heroes on a roster send the same bill.

**Stacked on #195 (`claude/ceramic-monorepo-map`), not on #194, for a stated reason.** No code here uses #195's code; the replay needs only the proposal tool from #194. But #195 claims file indices 012–014, moves the `.file-index-counter` to 014, and edits the same lines of the table of contents and README that this PR edits. Based on #194, this PR would either reuse #195's numbers or skip them. Either way it would conflict with #195 on the counter and the table of contents, and Ritz would have to resolve that by hand whichever merged second. Stacked on #195 it merges cleanly in order. None of #195's generated files are touched.

Before: the project claims that every change to an organisation is a diff somebody agreed to. Nothing checked that claim. A map edited by hand looked like any other map.

After: an org may keep `first.map`, the map as it was founded. `./replay-history ORG` starts there and applies every applied proposal again, in order. It judges each one as it stood on the day it was applied, and requires the result to be `org.map` byte for byte. Each way a history can fail to explain its map is refused by its code (H1–H7, now in document 003), and a mismatch prints the diff. `./run-tests` replays every example.

How: `src/015-history.lua` reuses the proposal tool's apply-and-judge code. `evaluate` gains an `as_of` date: it sets aside the `applied` line and every answer dated after that day. The proposal tool's `--write` now writes `applied DATE N`, where N is the org's change number. A new example, `examples/workshop/`, keeps a history: it was founded with two people, then Kai joins (change 1), then finishing becomes its own role between making and the buyer (change 2, a doors change with its outside eye and its week). A third proposal is still open. Both applied changes were made with `./apply-proposal --write`, not written by hand. The bakery gets a `first.map` equal to its map, since it has applied nothing. Issue 202 is complete.

Decisions:
- **History is opt-in, through `first.map`.** A generated map like the monorepo's keeps none, and that is not a fault.
- **The order is a change number on the `applied` line, not the date.** Two proposals applied the same day to the same block put their added lines down in the order they were applied, and a date cannot say which came first. N is optional in the format, so a history can be kept by hand. It is all-or-none (H2), runs 1..n once each (H3), and dates never go backwards in number order (H4). With no numbers at all, the order is inferred from dates and then names, with a warning (W4).
- **Each step is judged as it stood that day.** An approval written in afterwards does not make a change agreed after the fact (H6). The rules are the map's rules at that point in the replay.
- **A step that was not agreed is reported and the replay continues**, so one late approval does not hide a hand edit further on. A step that no longer applies stops the replay (H5), because nothing after it has a map to apply to.
- **The replay checks the map, not the state.** By design, state changes daily without proposals.

Tested: `tests/016-the-history.lua`, 18 checks. Each failure is made by tampering with a scratch copy of the real workshop history:
- a hand edit (H7)
- a back-dated approval (H6), with the step naming the unmet rule
- a door applied a day before its week was up (H6)
- swapped numbers (H4), a gap and a duplicate (H3), a mix of numbered and unnumbered (H2), and none numbered (W4)
- a change that no longer applies (H5)
- an invalid first map (H1)

All earlier suites still pass under LuaJIT and Lua 5.4 through `./run-tests`, which now also replays every example.

Issue 302: the energy menu is four buttons, in thirds. Stacked on #196 (301, mass income), which is stacked on #183.

## Before
The command door already had a `set-energy-level` verb, but it checked and stored the level itself. Nothing said what the levels mean, and nothing split engineers by the chosen level.

## After
- New module `src/051-energy-menu.lua`, with `.info.md`. It does not bootstrap a world and loads nothing:
  - `LEVELS` holds the four buttons, numbered 1 to 4: none, a third, two thirds and all. Each stores its share of engineers as a whole number of thirds (0 to 3), so the split is exact integer arithmetic.
  - `refusal(world, team, level)` returns the reason a level is refused (not a team in this match, or not button 1 to 4), or nil.
  - `set_level` raises `"energy-menu: " .. reason` on a refusal.
  - `level` reads a team's level back.
  - `split(world, team, engineers)` returns floor(engineers x thirds / 3) building, and the rest resting.
- `src/035-commands.lua`: the `set-energy-level` verb asks `menu.refusal` and then calls `menu.set_level`, so only one module knows what the buttons mean.

## How
The menu stores the level in the team's existing energy-level field, so the world layout, hash and copy do not change.

## Decisions
- **A stored 0 means no button has been pressed yet, and it reads as button 1, "none": nobody is on energy.** The issue's suite asks for exactly that ("with no button pressed yet, nobody is on energy"). A team keeps all its engineers on building until its player chooses.
- **`refusal` is exported.** The door can then refuse a command without raising, matching the other verbs.
- **`split` takes an engineer count, not a roster.** The roster is issue 304. Until it lands, the 302 suite reports ABSENT because it waits on `roster.on_energy`. I did not stub the roster to make it pass, and I did not change any assertion.

> **Merge #119 first.** This branch is built on `claude/040-claudemd-revisions`. Once #119 is merged, set this PR's base back to `main`.

**Why that base:** #119 is the lowest base this can honestly have. The tool needs only `libs/llama-chat-client.lua`, which is already on `main`, but its test needs the stand-in model, which #119 adds. The tool reads 049a's output *format* (the "left out" markers) but not its code, so it does not need #120.

## Before
The transcripts could be cut down by detail level (049a, #120), but they stayed conversation text. Nothing turned them into documentation for a given kind of reader.

## After
`scripts/abstraction-transform.lua TRANSCRIPT --level=high|medium|low` rewrites each exchange through the local model and puts the results into one Markdown document. The document has the spec's heading (`# NAME - HIGH Abstraction, Detail Level N`), a table of contents and numbered sections.
- **`--validate`** checks each rewrite, then retries up to three times and tells the model why the last answer was refused. The checks are:
  - no code outside low abstraction, and in low only at detail level 4–5;
  - high abstraction must name an input and an output;
  - the rewrite must keep at least a fifth of the original words.
- **Nothing is lost:** a chunk the model does not rewrite is kept word for word under `*[kept as written: REASON]*`. If the server can't be reached, the tool stops asking after the first timeout. Exit status 1 means no chunk got an answer.
- **`--cache=FILE`** stores rewrites keyed by text fingerprint and level, and only appends to the file.
- **`--compare-levels`** puts all three levels in one document.
- **Output:** `--out=FILE` writes to a file you name. `--write` writes to `llm-transcripts/generated/{level}-abstraction/`. Neither ever replaces a file. By default the document is only printed.

## How
- The prompts are in `config/abstraction-prompts.lua`, so their wording can be tuned without touching the code. `--prompts=FILE` uses another set.
- A section is one request together with its response. Sections longer than about 800 words are cut at paragraph breaks, never inside a ``` block.
- 049a's left-out markers are kept after the section they followed, and they set the detail level. `--detail=N` overrides that; with neither, the level is 5.

## Decisions
- The script lives at `scripts/abstraction-transform.lua`, as in the spec's CLI section. The spec's File Locations section says `scripts/libs/` instead.
- The unit of rewriting is the exchange, not each heading. A request on its own is usually too short to rewrite.
- **Key-term check** (second commit). Key terms are the names in backticks, file names, snake_case, camelCase and dotted names ("code"), plus acronyms of 3–5 capitals. Fenced code is left out. With `--validate`:
  - high abstraction may name none of the original's code names;
  - low must keep at least half of the key terms (when there are two or more);
  - medium is only counted, because matching ignores case but not synonyms, so a renamed concept counts as lost.

  `--report` gives each chunk's count, and the summary line gives the total.
- **Not edited here: `049-…viewer.md`, `PRIORITY.md` and `progress.md`.** #120 edits the same lines, so editing them here would cause conflicts. Only 049b's own issue file is updated: its Status section, plus 5 of 9 criteria ticked. The ones left are the checks on real model output.
- `brain.lua` was not edited, so this can't conflict with #120 or #155. The test works from the stand-in's default reply.

## Tested
- `test-abstraction-transform.sh --dir …`: **54/54 passed**, against the stand-in model. It covers rewriting, the marker on a model error, each validation rule including the key-term checks, cache reuse with the model gone, exit 1 with no model, compare mode, chunking, `--write`/`--out` refusals and usage errors.
- `validate-issues delta-version`: 93 findings before and after, the same set as on #119.
- Not run against the real Qwen3-8B server, which can't be reached from here.

**Stacked on #151** (`claude/tui-panels`, issue 048, renumbered from 039): this needs `tui.create_panel`. Merge #151 first; until then this diff also shows #151's commit.

Issue 045 (scripts): the menu's hand-placed layout moves onto tui panels. Follow-up filed as issue 046 (sections and items, after #93). The 3-row header for menus without a subtitle is filed as open issue 047, not built.

## Before:

`menu.lua` worked out every screen row by hand, and the numbers disagreed. The footer is 2 rows without shortcut keys and 3 with them, but the description and preview always stopped as if it were 3 (`footer_rows = 3`, `state.rows - 3`). So a menu without shortcut keys left an empty row above the footer and its preview lost a line. Titles were centred by their length in bytes, so a title with box characters or accents sat off centre, and a too-long title started left of the screen edge.

## After:

`menu.layout(rows, cols, {has_shortcuts=...})` splits the screen into **header** (rows 1-4), **footer** (the last 2 or 3 rows) and **body** panels once per redraw. The header and footer draw through their panels. The description and preview fill the body right down to the footer's top line. Titles and footer lines are centred by their width on screen and clipped to their panel.

New in `tui.lua`, asked for by delta-version's history viewer. **#189 could use both later:**
- `Panel:fill(char)` fills every visible cell in the current style, so a panel can be a coloured block. `Panel:clear` still leaves plain blanks.
- `tui.display_width(str)` and `tui.char_width(ch)` count terminal columns, not bytes: 0 for control, combining and zero-width characters, 2 for wide ones (CJK, Hangul, full-width forms, most emoji), 1 otherwise.

## How

- `menu.layout` is pure arithmetic, so it is testable with no terminal.
- A `footer_text` helper, split out of `render_footer`, tells `menu.render` the footer's height before anything is drawn.
- `render_description` and `render_content_source` stop at the body's last row.
- `test-menu-screen-replay.lua` takes an optional fourth argument, `all`, which prints blank rows too, so line N of its output is screen row N. Without it the output is unchanged.

## Decisions

- **Only the frame moves now.** Sections and items stay on screen rows, because #93 (`claude/menu-dropdown`) rewrites `render_item` and `render_section`. Moving them is issue 046, to do after #93 lands.
- **The body fills to the footer.** The old empty row came from the hard-coded 3, not from a wish for a gap; the footer's separator already divides the two.
- **The header stays 4 rows without a subtitle.** Shrinking it would move every menu's items up a row; that is a look change for its own issue.
- **Too-short screens:** the body keeps one row and the panels overlap. The tui drops whatever lands off screen.
- **`display_width` measures and does not change drawing.** The grid still holds one character per cell, so a wide character still pushes the rest of its row right.

## Conflicts

- **#93:** `git merge-tree` against `claude/menu-dropdown` is clean. I placed `menu.layout` after `render_header` so it doesn't collide with #93's new dropdown block. On the merged tree, both layout tests pass, and #93's own `test-menu-screen.sh` passes 36/0.
- **#179:** merges clean.
- **#162:** this branch does not edit `validate-issues`, so there is no conflict with it.

## Tested

- `luajit scripts/tests/test_menu-layout.lua "$PWD/scripts"`: 16/0. Covers footer heights, body bounds, row conversion, and tiny and zero-width screens.
- `bash scripts/tests/test-menu-layout.sh "$PWD/scripts"`: 9/0. Runs two real 24x80 menus with a 100-line preview, with and without a shortcut key, in a pretend terminal. Against the old `menu.lua`, "last preview line sits right above the footer" fails for the menu without a shortcut key; that is the bug this fixes.
- `luajit scripts/tests/test_tui-panels.lua "$PWD/scripts"`: 58/0, with 14 new checks for `fill` and `display_width`.
- `bash scripts/libs/test-menu-screen.sh "$PWD/scripts/libs"`: 7/0, unchanged.

**Stacked on #194 (`claude/ceramic-proposals`)**, which stacks on #193 and #192. It shares the project's file-index counter with them, so it cannot stand alone.

Before: the tools had only a made-up bakery to read. Nothing could tell the person who merges in this monorepo which of the waiting pull requests frees the most work.

After: the monorepo's own queue is an org. `./map-the-monorepo --fetch` takes a snapshot of every open pull request and the projects it touches, through GitHub's REST API, reading only. It writes the map, validates it, and writes `examples/monorepo/board.txt` and `page.html`. Then it prints the merges and answers that can be done now, ranked by how much waits behind each. Today's snapshot (2026-11-03) has 184 open pull requests, 80 of which can be merged now. **The top of the board is #63** (RPG-autobattler mana bars), the bottom of a stack that 22 boxes wait behind. Next come #116 (supcom dunes) and #2 (gif-generator 701a), each reaching 14. Any org can also be written as a static HTML5 page with no JavaScript (`./org-page`). Phase 1 is complete, with `./run-phase-demo 1`.

How: `scripts/list-open-pull-requests` (Bash) takes the snapshot. `src/012-monorepo-map.lua` converts the snapshot plus a hand-kept `input/questions` into `org.map`, deterministically. `src/013-org-page.lua` writes the page. The board gains `--says`, which prints each row's title under it. Issues 105 and 106 are complete, with the phase 1 demo.

Decisions:
- **Pull requests and questions are work boxes held by the owner. Projects are roles held by the builder.** A project box means "its next round of work". It waits on every open pull request touching it, because the next round branches from main.
- **A stacked pull request waits on the one it is built on.** One built on a branch no open pull request carries gets its base as a *fixed value* naming the branch. Nothing blocks it but retargeting, so it should not rank as a blocker.
- **Projects are read from changed files' top-level directories**, not titles. Two directories that would get one map name are refused, not merged.
- **Only three questions are listed.** They are the ones whose own project files say they are open and waiting on the owner: soren-ds's catalogue question, and this project's Q1 (soramech) and trainstation question. I did not guess at every open question in every project.
- **The snapshot is committed with its date.** A test checks that the committed map, board and both pages are exactly what their inputs make, byte for byte.
- **The page shows the board first**, then every box with each wire a link to the other end and each waiting port marked. Following links from the top row walks the chain by hand. It refuses an invalid org rather than drawing something untrue.

Tested: `tests/014-the-monorepo-and-the-page.lua`, 38 checks, plus the earlier suites, all passing under LuaJIT and Lua 5.4 via `./run-tests`. Name mapping and quoting round-trip. A fixture queue covers the stack, an orphaned base, root files, questions, determinism and board order, and the refusals are tested. The generated examples are checked against their generators. For the page: no script, no event handlers, every link lands (1382 on the monorepo page, none broken), and escaping holds. `./run-phase-demo 1` runs end to end.

**Stacked on #193 (`claude/ceramic-reader-and-board`)**, whose reader it uses. That one is stacked on the data-model PR.

Before: proposals, the organisation's pull requests, were specified and nothing read them. So the rulings in document 003 were positions on paper.

After: `./apply-proposal ORG PROPOSAL` prints a proposal's derived status: ready, waiting, stale, broken, invalid, withdrawn or applied. It also prints the change id, the kinds of change, who each kind affects, every rule and whether it is met, each person's standing answer, any state the change would make untrue, and the unified diff of `org.map`. `--write` applies a ready proposal. `--today` fixes the date, so results are reproducible.

How: `src/010-proposals.lua` reads the proposal (P1–P6). It applies the line edits to the map's *text*, putting untouched lines back byte for byte. It validates the result with the same reader, carries the state across, and judges each kind against the rules in force before the change. Document 003 is sharpened where building it found ambiguity. Issue 104 is complete.

Decisions:
- **LINE is compared character for character** with the map's body line. Field-wise matching would let two spellings both match.
- **`+` lines go after the last body line the block still has.** Tidying happens only where something was removed, so the diff holds only the change.
- **An answer from somebody not in the org is shown and not counted**, rather than making the proposal invalid. Otherwise a stranger could block anything by appending a line.
- **A proposal by somebody not in the org, that does not add them, is invalid.**
- **`--write` refuses anything but ready.** It marks the proposal `applied` rather than moving it.
- **An objection from somebody the change does not affect** is printed as "on the record, and not blocking". This makes the route-around rule visible: Dee objects to Ana rewiring the oven money, and Dee isn't asked.
- **Exit 3 means "not ready"**, distinct from 1 (error) and 2 (usage).

Tested: `tests/011-proposals.lua`, 60 checks, all passing under LuaJIT and Lua 5.4. They cover the FNV-1a published vectors and document 003's example id, and both bakery proposals. They cover stale, broken, invalid and withdrawn. They check **each ruling**: a consumer routes around a producer without asking, a new wire needs both ends, a change inside your box needs you, you can leave alone, and nobody is put in a box without saying yes. A door needs an outside eye and a week, and joining needs a sponsor. A rules change is judged by the old rules (2/3 and 30 days by default, everyone if the map says so). An approval naming another change id does not count. A rewired port's `fed` line is dropped. `--write` was also exercised on a copy of the bakery.

Before: the org map was a specification with nothing reading it, so "everyone can see what's blocking" was only a promise.

After: `./validate-org ORG` checks an org against every rule in document 002. It names every problem with its file, line and rule code, not only the first, and prints warnings separately. `./blocked-board ORG` ranks every source of waiting by reach, then frees, then whether someone can act now. `--ready` shows only what somebody can deliver today. `./run-tests` runs every test under LuaJIT and then under Lua 5.4.

Run directly, it is the validator. `src/008-blocked-board.lua` computes owes, frees and reach exactly as document 004 defines them. Each module has its `.info.md` companion, and the scripts follow the hard-coded `DIR` plus override idiom. Issues 102 and 103 are complete.

- **The reader and the validator are one module.** Every check is something a reader must refuse anyway. A second reading of the same file could disagree with the first.
- **A stray `#` after a line's fields is refused as L9**, so the code points at the actual mistake. A refusal points at the offending line, not the block's head.
- **Lines are kept with their text and number**, blank and comment lines included, because the proposal tool edits the text.
- **Reach before frees.** At the bottom of a stack of ten, frees is 1 and reach is 9.
